items.title: BLS: U.S. Economy Adds 29,000 Jobs in September, Falling Short of Expectations
items.description: WASHINGTON, D.C. — The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) has reported that the U.S. economy added 29,000 jobs in September. This figure falls short of the roughly 84,000 new jobs estimated for the month by Dow Jones economists, according to CNBC. Meanwhile, the U.S. unemployment rate has slightly increased to 4.2 percent. The BLS has also downwardly revised the July job gains from +21,000 to -10,000 and the August gains from +162,000 to +133,000, totaling 60,000 fewer jobs than previously reported in those two months. items.title: What's next for housing: 7%, 8% or 9% mortgage rates?
items.description: Halloween is coming early for the housing market. The bond market has been very scary for weeks now, but last week was so wild that we can actually talk about what is more likely now: mortgage rates at 7%, 8% or 9%? Let’s take a drive down to scary-rate lane, where Chuckie will be our driver, Jason will be sitting in the back seat and Freddy Krueger will be waiting for us to fall asleep. 10-year yield and mortgage rates In the 2026 HousingWire forecast , I anticipated the following ranges: Mortgage rates between 5.75% and 6.75% The 10-year yield fluctuating between 3.80% and 4.60% I believe two events have made the bond market act more wildly than normal: First, the MOU deal with Iran fell apart, and we started attacking Iran during market hours. Second, President Trump said we won’t get a deal with Iran until after the midterms. With no sign of the Iran conflict ending, the bond market has acted up, even as we get more oil through the Strait of Hormuz. Let’s look at the possibility of each rate level. 7% mortgage rates The case for 7% rates is very simple: the conflict ends and Trade War 2.0 doesn’t get worse — those two things alone can drive the 10-year yield and mortgage rates back to 7%. But the market has to really believe this conflict is over and we need diesel prices back down again. With the Federal Reserve members blinking at higher rates, this outcome toward 7% is more likely now. 8% mortgage rates A few weeks ago I wrote about what could get us to 8% mortgage rates; we would need the 10-year yield to get toward 5.40% and mortgage spreads to get worse. This level would also require strong economic data, a hawkish Fed and the conflict to keep going. We had all of these things to push yields higher, but mortgage spreads didn’t get worse enough last week and Friday’s jobs report missed estimates . So, 5.40% on the 10-year yield wasn’t high enough: we would need higher yields or worse spreads to get to 8%. 9% mortgage rates Last week I wrote about the possibility of 9% mortgage rates, and thankfully, it would take a lot of work to get there. Nominal growth needs to be between 5%-8% every quarter, there can’t be any softness in the labor market, no Fed members can blink on rate hikes and the Fed hawks would need to ask for more rate hikes than they currently are. Plus, the conflict would need to last much longer than expected. Together, these factors could push mortgage rates toward 9%. If mortgage spreads were at 3.47% today, not 2.04%, then mortgage rates would be 9% already. Mortgage spreads Mortgage spreads are now front and center and the most important housing story. If spreads worsen, the housing market could get much worse, affecting not only existing home sales but also housing starts for years to come. For now, the spreads have behaved like they typically do, but this is something to keep an eye on in the future. However, the move from year-to-date lows to today isn’t extreme. Historically, mortgage spreads have ranged from 1.60% to 1.80%. Last week, spreads rose to 2.04%, up from 1.98% the week before. Let’s compare last week’s mortgage rates to where they would have been over the last three years, given the 10-year yield’s current level: If we had the worst mortgage spread levels of 2023, mortgage rates would be 8.64% today, not 7.57%. If we had the worst levels of 2024, mortgage rates would be 8.26% today. If we had the worst levels of 2025, mortgage rates would be 8.07% today. Housing inventory Housing inventory growth has been very tame this year, with certain weeks being negative year over year. As always, it’s been hard to get inventory growth when mortgage demand is rising; it’s easier when mortgage demand is declining. With mortgage rates over 7.50%, demand is getting hit and the rise in inventory has a bit more kick. Housing weekly inventory grew 0.75% — or 6,714 homes — but it’s late in the year, similar to 2023, when rates approached 8%. The seasonal peak will happen in October or

items.title: Private listing ecosystems could deepen the housing affordability crisis
items.description: It was encouraging to see lawmakers make good on their promise to prioritize homeownership earlier this year with the bipartisan passage of the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act. But more than two months later, it has become clear that the current home affordability crisis goes beyond building more units, and the initial adjustments to macroeconomic levers will not be enough to avoid a fundamental crisis of opportunity in the housing market. In the last few months, traditional housing inventory has increased yet, the median existing-home price also increased for the 38th consecutive month on a year-over-year basis. Existing-home sales fell another 2% in August to an annualized rate of 3.98 million, while pending sales remained 4.7% below last year’s level. The new law was a starting point, not the solution. Americans are still confronting a housing market characterized by historically depressed sales activity, elevated borrowing costs and persistently high home prices. Addressing those challenges requires looking beyond simply building more homes and adjusting macroeconomic levers to the structural factors that determine whether consumers can actually access the housing opportunities that exist. For millions of Americans, homeownership no longer feels like a realistic milestone, with the median age of first-time U.S. homebuyers reaching an all-time high of 40. Elevated mortgage rates , rising construction costs, persistent inflation and economic uncertainty have combined to create one of the most hostile housing environments in modern memory. These conditions are daunting, but they also present a profound opportunity. This moment demands structural intervention to restore the basic accessibility that American families deserve. Lawmakers should be applauded for coming together to pass the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, but their work is far from done in order to restore affordability in the housing market. While economists watch interest rates and advocacy groups push for local zoning reforms, a critical structural shift is happening right before our eyes. It has been completely overlooked by policymakers and remains under the radar of most consumers. It is a quiet war over data, transparency, and market access. The rise of closed ecosystems For years, policymakers have scrutinized transparency and competition in financial markets, social media platforms, and the healthcare industry. Yet there has been very little attention paid to transparency in the housing market, even though homeownership remains the primary source of wealth creation for most American families. Right now, the residential real estate market is experiencing a dangerous shift toward fragmentation, reduced visibility, and closed listing ecosystems. What was once a transparent marketplace is splintering into private networks. We have recently experienced the temporary disappearance of thousands of Chicago-area listings from public platforms, with the threat of more to follow; a controversy surrounding the largest real estate company’s private-listing strategy; and regulatory scrutiny that has raised broader questions about transparency and competition. This has led multiple states to introduce legislation that regulates private listings. At the same time, a Consumer Policy Center report found elevated levels of double-ended transactions among certain brokerage models, renewing concerns that reduced competition and self-serving business practices are preventing consumers from benefiting from the openness and competition that healthy housing markets require. This structural shift limits the consumer’s ability to see all the available homes on the market. As a result, this creates an illusion of limited supply, making it more difficult for consumers to identify newly available homes and limiting access to those properties to a smaller group of people. Big-ticket item purchases have fallen sharply at Lowe's and Home Depot. Mortgage rates hit their highest level in three years this week, above 7.5%, and according to home services platform Angi, many homeowners are staying in their current houses five years longer than they originally planned. In this article HD Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Courtneyk | E+ | Getty Images With mortgage rates continuing to stay untenably high for most Americans, many are staying put. But that doesn't mean homes don't need improving and upkeep. And some homeowners figure that if they can't move into a new home, they'll make their old home newer — a new deck or perhaps a walk-in closet. Traditionally, a home equity loan or home equity line of credit would be the first tool to reach for. But even those are getting too expensive for homeowners. This leaves homeowners effectively trapped in aging homes with no easy way out, or way to improve them. And even when homeowners are tapping into home equity loans — homeowners did originate nearly 20% more second mortgages or HELOCs in the second quarter of this year compared with the first quarter — they likely aren't using the equity for improvements. Experts say they are using them to stay afloat. Untapped or expensive, Americans are sitting on a record amount of home equity . As rates keep rising, tapping into home equity will become more and more expensive for homeowners. This will generally hold back consumer spending, but it will hit big-ticket items, like home renovations, particularly hard, said Tom Graff, chief investment officer of Facet, a financial planning and wealth management firm. This struggle is something built into the rate hikes, according to Graff. The Fed is hiking interest rates in an attempt to control inflation. One of the ways that is supposed to work is by pushing down consumer spending. So the fact that consumers will struggle to finance large purchases is by design, he said. items.title: How United Apartment Group plans to hit 50k units under management
items.description: An article from How United Apartment Group plans to hit 50,000 units under management New hires Woody Stone and Lenzie O’Connor bring decades of experience to the San Antonio-based operator, as it also seeks acquisition opportunities in markets like Charlotte, North Carolina. Published Oct. 2, 2026 Leslie Shaver Senior Reporter Share Copy link Email LinkedIn X/Twitter Facebook Print License Add us on Google Mason Park, in Houston, Texas. Permission granted by United Apartment Group United Apartment Group just missed the most recent National Multifamily Housing Council Top 50 managers list after appearing on the previous nine lists. If CEO Tim Settles and President Loyal Proffitt have their way, the San Antonio-based firm will be on the NMHC’s annual list in future years. UAG, which has 32,237 units under management, is eyeing 35,000 by year-end and 50,000 by 2030 as it aims to move into new markets to meet client needs and enter its next phase of growth. “Historically, as we've grown the company, it's really been organically — existing clients, broker referrals, and things of that nature,” Settles, founder and CEO of UAG, told Multifamily Dive. To get there, it brought in two well-known industry veterans in September, hiring Woody Stone as chief growth officer and Lenzie O’Connor as vice president of client services and strategy, according to a press release. Further, the 31-year-old apartment operator is also seeking merger-and-acquisition opportunities to fuel its growth strategy. Meeting partner client needs In 2020, Brixton Capital acquired a majority interest in UAG . The Solana Beach, California-based private real estate investment company is the engine behind UAG’s growth goals, according to Proffitt. “They [Brixton] want to scale their portfolio on the acquisition side of things, but also want the management company to expand its footprint,” Proffitt said. “It's not only about growing in number of units.” Instead, the bigger driver is expanding the number of markets UAG operates in so it can better serve existing clients as they continue to buy deals, while also managing Brixton’s growing portfolio. “We've got clients that are in other markets,” Proffitt told Multifamily Dive. “As we grow the portfolio, that creates opportunities for our associates to be able to move to other markets to be able to be promoted.” While UAG will continue to “mine for clients,” it's also interested in buying other management firms in the 3,000- to 10,000-unit range to scale, according to Proffitt. Currently, the company has a sizable footprint in Texas. “We'd like to go into Charlotte, [North Carolina],” Proffitt said. “We'd like to get into Denver. We'd like to get into Phoenix, Vegas and deeper into Atlanta, deeper into Nashville and deeper into Florida. In some ways, we can do that by buying other management companies.” Over the years, a number of ownership groups have added management platforms. But some of those companies decide to jettison operations due to the difficulty finding employees or not having the economies of scale, Proffitt said. “They end up spending a lot of time on the management side of things and not buying deals or not raising money,” Proffitt said. “They end up just kind of kicking out because they can't make it work. We're definitely in the market for some groups like that.” Stone, O’Connor add decades of experience Stone, with 25 years in the industry, is no newcomer in property management leadership circles. He previously served as president of Multifamily Asset Services for Cushman Wakefield, where he provided strategic oversight for its management platform with approximately 180,000 units, per the release. Before then, he was at Pinnacle, which Cushman Wakefield bought in 2020 , holding a variety of roles. After Cushman, he founded Stone Advisory Group, where he advised private equity firms, institutional multifamily organizations and proptech companies. items.title: Tiger Woods Spearheads Gated Golf Community in Texas with Luxury Homes Starting at $1M
items.description: Real Estate News Follow Us On Google Tiger Woods Spearheads Gated Golf Community in Texas with Luxury Homes Starting at $1M By Kiri Blakeley October 3, 2026 Realtor.com / Getty Images / Bluejack A luxury residential golf community spearheaded by golf legend Tiger Woods is opening this fall outside of Fort Worth, TX . Bluejack Ranch is the 914-acre followup to Bluejack National, a highly-rated resort-style community and private club three hours away in Montgomery, which is the first Tiger Woods-designed golf course in the country. Eventually, the new $2.5 billion Bluejack Ranch community will have 500 custom and semi-custom homes, ranging from 1,282 square foot, 2-bedroom casitas to estate homes on one-half to one-acre sites with a minimum of 4,000 square feet. There's also the occasional sprawling mansions, at 19,000-plus square feet, which can run into the tens of millions. Prices start at $775,000 for half-acre lots on which to build and residential products start at $1M, with an average home costing between $2 million and $4 million. Lot buyers must use a Bluejack builder. "You live on 900 acres with every form of entertainment imaginable," developer Andy Mitchell tells Realtor.com. "You don't need a big home, necessarily. It's like going to a resort, you don't have to build your own game room." Loading... Pro golfer "J.J." Henry (left), developer Andy Mitchell (center) and golf icon Tiger Woods (right) partnered on creating private residential golf communities Bluejack National and now Bluejack Ranch, both in central Texas. Katie Park The courses, designed by Woods' TGR Design firm and land planner Beau Welling , a firm based in Greenville, SC , has a championship 18-hole course as well as a "short course" with 10 holes, and a practice facility with driving range and three putting greens. The standard course will stretch over almost 8,000 yards from the "Tiger tees" or longest tee boxes. It has been grassed with Stadium Zoysia. Located in Aledo—a 20 minute drive from downtown Fort Worth—the community will also boast a private golf club, a working dude ranch, entertainment hall, podcast studios, multiple pools, tennis and pickleball courts, bowling alley, several restaurants, comfort stations, a spa and wellness center, all ages recreational center, and a 24/7 gated security. The developer is also planning a commercial hub near the front "greeter's barn," filled with what the developer hopes will be "high-end lifestyle brands" that will suit the community theme of "laidback luxury." Building a Bluejack brand Loading... The developer offers multiple styles of homes, and the entry price point is around $1 million. Bluejack Bluejack Ranch developer Andy Mitchell , co-chairman and co-owner, with wife Kristin Mitchell, of Bluejack Management Partners , first met golf legend Tiger Woods in 2013. "He was just kicking off his design business," says Mitchell. A mutual friend brought the pair together for a collaboration that led to Bluejack National, Woods' first U.S. design project. (He had already worked on one in Cabo San Lucas, Mexico.) "We're both fathers, our kids are similar age," says Mitchell. "We're literally one month apart. We're a lot alike. We both love to win. I can't hide it, he can't hide it." "If we're going to do something, he wants it to be the best." The developer says while both he and Woods were concerned about the courses, an even greater goal was integrating family into the community, making it a truly multigenerational experience. To that end, there's a slew of amenities for kids and those who don't tee off. Mitchell stresses that the community will be the type of place where someone as famous as Woods can walk around or have dinner without being pestered for a selfie. "You're free to be Tiger Woods ," he says of the community. "Nobody is going to solicit you or ask for your autograph. If someone were to walk up to Tiger when he's having dinner with his two kids, they wouldn't be a member tomorrow morning."

items.title: Why Underserved Housing Markets Are Drawing Real Estate Investors – BNO News
items.description: Reviews Why Underserved Housing Markets Are Drawing Real Estate Investors Published on September 29, 2026 By Contributor Credit: Oleksandr Pidvalnyi Share Tweet The real estate markets that generate the most media coverage – gateway cities, luxury segments, coastal markets – aren’t where a growing share of investment capital is going. Investors are increasingly directing attention toward smaller cities, secondary metros, and markets that have historically been underserved by both institutional capital and the construction pipelines that serve higher-income demand. The reasons are both financial and structural. The Supply-Demand Gap That Creates Opportunity ECA Holdings represents a category of investor operating in markets where the gap between housing supply and housing demand has been left largely unaddressed by conventional development activity. In markets like smaller North Carolina cities, that gap is substantial. Population growth driven by job creation in logistics, manufacturing, and healthcare has outpaced housing supply in ways that create persistent demand without the supply response that higher-cost markets attract. The basic economics are straightforward. When the gap between demand and supply stays open, vacancy stays low and rents hold. There’s no competing pipeline absorbing the demand that keeps your units full. For investors focused on residential and workforce housing, that dynamic translates to more predictable income streams and lower vacancy risk than in saturated markets. The conventional real estate investment thesis has long centered on appreciation in high-cost markets. The alternative thesis that’s drawing capital to underserved markets is centered on yield – the income generated relative to acquisition cost. In markets where home values and rents reflect local incomes rather than speculation, acquisition costs are lower and cap rates are higher. A property that generates a 7 percent cap rate in a secondary market competes differently against institutional-grade assets in primary markets than a sub-4 percent cap rate property ever could. What makes underserved markets attractive to value-focused investors: Higher cap rates – acquisition costs relative to net operating income produce returns that primary markets can rarely match, particularly for smaller investors without access to institutional leverage Lower competition – institutional buyers focused on scale and liquidity tend to avoid smaller markets, reducing the bidding pressure that compresses returns in gateway cities Stable demand from workforce population – healthcare workers, teachers, logistics employees, and manufacturing workers need housing close to employment centers in exactly the markets that institutional capital has historically underserved Longer hold periods supported by demographics – secondary metros that are growing due to job creation rather than speculation tend to have more durable demand bases than speculative markets The Risks That Require Understanding Investing in underserved markets isn’t without complexity. The same factors that create yield opportunity also create risks that don’t exist or are less pronounced in primary markets. Liquidity is the most significant risk. A property in a secondary market takes longer to sell and attracts fewer buyers than an equivalent property in a major metro. Investors who need to exit quickly face a much thinner buyer pool and potentially significant price concessions. This makes underserved market investment better suited to investors with longer time horizons and lower liquidity needs. Property management is another genuine challenge. Major metros have deep pools of professional property management companies with scale and systems. In smaller markets, management quality is more variable and capacity is more constrained.
